subject: math
title: Probability: Probability Lines, Fractions, Decimals, Percents and Two Independent Events
seo_title: Grade 6 Probability Worksheets: Probability Line, Tree Diagrams and Experiments (Free, Answer Key)
standard_text: Use fractions, decimals, and percents to express the probability of events happening, represent this probability on a probability line, and use it to make predictions and informed decisions; determine and compare the theoretical and experimental probabilities of two independent events happening
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 math worksheets on probability for the Ontario curriculum: the probability line from 0 to 1, probability as a fraction, decimal and percent, spinners, number cubes and bags, two independent events with tables and tree diagrams, and theoretical vs experimental probability. 100 questions with an answer key, good EQAO practice.
key_big: A probability is a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain): the outcomes you want ÷ all the outcomes.
key_sub: 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. A coin and a number cube give 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes, not 2 + 6. More trials get closer to the theory, and a coin has no memory: after 5 tails, heads is still 1/2.
body_html:
The probability line

A probability is a number from 0 to 1. 0 means impossible. 1 means certain. Halfway, 12 or 0.5, means equally likely to happen or not. A probability is never more than 1.

The same probability can be written as a fraction, a decimal or a percent. As a percent, the line goes from 0% to 100%.

FractionDecimalPercentChance
000%impossible
140.2525%unlikely
120.550%equally likely
340.7575%likely
11100%certain

Working out a probability

When the outcomes are equally likely:

probability = number of outcomes you want ÷ total number of outcomes

Example 1

What is the probability of taking a red marble from this bag?

There are 3 red marbles and 8 marbles altogether. Compare with all 8, not with the 5 blue.

Answer: 38 = 0.375 = 37.5%

Two independent events

Two events are independent when one does not change the chance of the other, like tossing a coin and spinning a spinner. List every outcome in a tree diagram or a table. The number of outcomes is found by multiplying: 2 coin faces × 3 colours = 6 outcomes.

Example 2

You toss a coin and spin the spinner (red, blue, yellow, all equal). What is the probability of tails and blue?

The tree has 6 outcomes. Only one of them is T, blue.

Answer: 16

Example 3

What is the probability of heads and an even number?

Find H2, H4 and H6 in the table: 3 of the 12 outcomes.

Answer: 312 = 14 = 25%

Theoretical and experimental probability

The theoretical probability is what should happen, found by counting outcomes. The experimental probability is what did happen: number of times it happened ÷ number of trials. They are usually close, but rarely exactly the same. More trials usually get closer.

Coin tossesHeadsExperimental probability
107710 = 0.7
1004646100 = 0.46
10005085081000 = 0.508
Example 4

You roll a number cube 60 times. About how many 6s would you expect?

A 6 has probability 16. 16 of 60 is 60 ÷ 6 = 10.

Answer: about 10

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
“The probability is 1.2.”Probabilities are never more than 1 (100%).
3 red, 5 blue, so P(red) = 35.Divide by ALL the outcomes: 38.
A coin and a number cube give 2 + 6 = 8 outcomes.Multiply: 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes.
“5 tails in a row, so heads is due.”A coin has no memory. Heads is still 12.

faq.q: What do Grade 6 students learn about probability in the Ontario math curriculum?
faq.a: In Grade 6 (Data, D2), students write probabilities as fractions, decimals and percents, place them on a probability line from 0 to 1, and use them to make predictions and decisions. They also find and compare the theoretical and experimental probabilities of two independent events, such as tossing a coin and spinning a spinner.
Two events are independent when one does not change the chance of the other. Tossing a coin and rolling a number cube are independent: getting heads does not make a 6 more or less likely.

faq.q: How do you find the probability of two independent events in Grade 6?
faq.a: List every outcome in a tree diagram or a table, then count. A coin and a number cube give 2 × 6 = 12 equally likely outcomes, so heads and a 6 has a probability of 1/12.

faq.q: What is the difference between theoretical and experimental probability?
faq.a: Theoretical probability is what should happen, found by counting outcomes. Experimental probability is what actually happened in trials, such as 23 heads in 50 tosses (23/50). With more trials, the two usually get closer.

items.q: What is the probability of an event that is impossible?
items.e: An impossible event can never happen, so its probability is 0. 0.1 is very unlikely, but it can still happen.

items.q: What is the probability of an event that is certain?
items.e: A certain event will happen, so its probability is 1 (or 100%). The number 100 on its own is far bigger than 1, so it can’t be a probability.

items.q: An event is equally likely to happen or not happen. What is its probability?
items.e: Equally likely is halfway between 0 and 1: 12 (0.5 or 50%). 2 is the number of outcomes, not the probability.

items.q: Which number can NOT be a probability?
items.e: Probabilities go from 0 to 1. 1.5 is bigger than 1, so it can’t be a probability. 0 and 1 are allowed: they mean impossible and certain.

items.q: Which percent can NOT be a probability?
items.e: As a percent, probabilities go from 0% to 100%. 120% is more than 100%, so it is not possible.

items.q: Which word best describes the chance shown by the arrow?
items.e: The arrow is at 0.8. That is between 0.5 and 1, close to 1: likely. It is not certain, because it is not at 1.

items.q: Which word best describes the chance shown by the arrow?
items.e: The arrow is at 0.1, close to 0 but not at 0: unlikely. Impossible would be exactly 0.

items.q: Which probability means an event is very likely?
items.e: 0.95 is very close to 1, so the event is very likely. 0.05 is very close to 0 (very unlikely). 9.5 is bigger than 1, so it is not a probability.

items.q: Which probability shows the most likely event?
items.e: Compare the tenths: 0.8 = 0.80 is the greatest. 0.35 has more digits, but 0.35 < 0.80. So 0.8 is most likely.

items.q: Which probability shows the least likely event?
items.e: Write them with two decimal places: 0.05, 0.50, 0.15, 0.30. The least is 0.05, so that event is least likely.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a 7?
items.e: The cube only has 1 to 6, so a 7 is impossible. Its probability is 0.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a number from 1 to 6?
items.e: Every roll gives a number from 1 to 6, so it is certain: 1. 6 is the number of outcomes, and probabilities are never more than 1.

items.q: The probability line is split into quarters. What probability does the arrow show?
items.e: There are 4 equal parts from 0 to 1, and the arrow is 1 part from 0: 14 (0.25). 34 counts from the 1 end. 14 is 0.25, not 0.4.

items.q: The probability line is split into tenths. What probability does the arrow show?
items.e: Each small step is 0.1. The arrow is 7 steps from 0, so it shows 0.7. 0.3 counts back from 1. 7 is too big to be a probability.

items.q: What probability does the arrow show, as a percent?
items.e: The arrow is at 0.3. 0.3 = 30 hundredths = 30%. 3% would be 0.03.

items.q: Owen says the probability that his hockey team wins on Saturday is 1.2, because they are very good. What is wrong?
c: A probability can’t be more than 1
Nothing, strong teams can go above 1
items.e: Even a certain event has probability 1 (100%). A probability can’t be more than 1. A very good team might be 0.8 or 0.9: likely, not certain.

items.q:
Which list orders these probabilities from least likely to most likely?
0.6, 0.25, 0.9, 0.06
items.e: Write them as hundredths: 0.60, 0.25, 0.90, 0.06. Least to greatest: 0.06, 0.25, 0.6, 0.9. 0.25 is less than 0.6, even though 25 is more than 6.

items.q: A bag has 3 red and 7 blue marbles. You take one without looking. Which letter shows the probability of taking a red marble?
items.e: 3 of the 10 marbles are red: 310 = 0.3. That is point B. C (0.7) is the probability of blue.

items.q: A spinner has 10 equal sections: 7 green and 3 yellow. Which letter shows the probability of landing on green?
items.e: 7 of the 10 equal sections are green: 710 = 0.7. That is point C.

items.q: Arjun estimates the probability of four events. Which estimate makes the most sense?
c: rolling a 6 on a number cube: 0.6
snow on the ground in Winnipeg on January 15: 0.9
items.e: Winnipeg almost always has snow on the ground in January, so 0.9 (very likely) makes sense. A coin is about 0.5 for heads, a 6 is only 16 (about 0.17), and snow in Toronto in July is close to 0. So the answer is snow in Winnipeg in January.

sets.title: Probability as a fraction, decimal and percent

items.q: The probability of heads is 12. What is this as a decimal?
items.e: 12 = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5. Writing the digits 1 and 2 as 0.12 or 1.2 is a common mistake.

items.q: The probability of landing on blue is 14. What is this as a percent?
items.e: 14 = 25100 = 25%. 14% just writes the digits 1 and 4.

items.q: Write the probability 310 as a decimal.
items.e: 310 is 3 tenths = 0.3. 0.03 is 3 hundredths.

items.q: Write the probability 0.75 as a percent.
items.e: To change a decimal to a percent, multiply by 100: 0.75 × 100 = 75%.

items.q: Which fraction is equal to the probability 0.2?
items.e: 0.2 = 210 = 15. 12 is 0.5, and 2100 is 0.02.

items.q: Write the probability 15 as a percent.
items.e: 15 = 20100 = 20%. Multiply the numerator and denominator by 20.

items.q: Write the probability 910 as a decimal.
items.e: 910 is 9 tenths = 0.9. 0.1 is the probability that the event does NOT happen.

items.q: Write the probability 35 as a percent.
items.e: 35 = 60100 = 60%. Multiply the numerator and denominator by 20.

items.q: Write the probability 40% as a fraction in lowest terms.
items.e: 40% = 40100. Divide the numerator and denominator by 20: 25. 4100 would be 4%.

items.q: Write the probability 0.05 as a percent.
Write the probability 18 as a decimal.
items.e: 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125. A quick check: 14 = 0.25, and 18 is half of that.

items.q: Write the probability 720 as a percent.
items.e: Multiply the numerator and denominator by 5: 720 = 35100 = 35%. 27% comes from adding 7 + 20.

items.q: Write the probability 1225 as a decimal.
items.e: Multiply the numerator and denominator by 4: 1225 = 48100 = 0.48. 0.37 comes from adding 12 + 25.

items.q: Write the probability 68 as a percent.
items.e: 68 = 34 = 75%. 68% just writes the digits 6 and 8.

items.q: The weather forecast says there is a 30% chance of snow. What is this as a decimal?
items.e: 30% = 30100 = 0.3. Divide by 100 to change a percent to a decimal.

items.q: Which of these is NOT equal to a probability of 12?
items.e: 12 = 0.5 = 50% = 24. 0.2 is 15, not a half.

items.q: Which of these is NOT equal to a probability of 34?
items.e: 34 = 0.75 = 75% = 68. 0.34 just writes the digits 3 and 4; it is not 34.

items.q: Which shows the probability of landing on blue as a fraction, a decimal and a percent?
items.e: Blue covers one quarter of the spinner: 14 = 0.25 = 25%. 12 is the probability of red. 14 is 0.25, not 0.4 or 0.14.

items.q: Which probability is the greatest?
items.e: Change them all to decimals: 34 = 0.75, 0.7 = 0.70, 72% = 0.72, 0.69. The greatest is 34.

items.q: Which list orders these probabilities from least to greatest?
items.e: Change them to decimals: 14 = 0.25, 0.3 = 0.30, 35% = 0.35. So the order is 14, 0.3, 35%. 14 is 0.25, not 0.4.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a 4?
items.e: There are 6 equally likely outcomes and only one of them is 4: 16. 46 would be the chance of 1, 2, 3 or 4.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling an even number?
items.e: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6: 3 of the 6 outcomes, so 36 (= 12). 63 is upside down: it is greater than 1.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4?
items.e: Greater than 4 means 5 or 6: 2 of the 6 outcomes, so 26. 36 wrongly includes the 4. 16 forgets the 5.

items.q: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue marbles. You take one without looking. What is the probability of red?
items.e: There are 3 + 5 = 8 marbles and 3 are red: 38. 35 compares red with blue, not with all the marbles. Two colours does not mean 12.

items.q: You take one marble without looking. What is the probability of blue?
items.e: There are 4 + 2 + 2 = 8 marbles and 2 are blue: 28 (= 14). 26 compares blue with the other 6 marbles, not with all 8. 48 is red.

items.q: What is the probability of landing on red?
items.e: Red covers half of the spinner: 12. 13 counts the colours, but the sections are not equal.

items.q: The spinner has 8 equal sections: G is green and Y is yellow. What is the probability of green?
items.e: 3 of the 8 equal sections are green: 38. 35 compares green with yellow. 58 is yellow.

items.q: A spinner has 10 equal sections: 3 blue and 7 red. What is the probability of blue as a decimal?
items.e: 3 of the 10 sections are blue: 310 = 0.3. 0.7 is the probability of red.

items.q: A bag has 20 marbles and 5 of them are green. What is the probability of green as a percent?
items.e: 520 = 25100 = 25%. 5% uses the number of green marbles as the percent. 75% is NOT green.

items.q: A bag has 3 red and 7 yellow marbles. What is the probability of NOT getting red?
items.e: Not red means yellow: 7 of the 10 marbles, so 710. Check: 310 + 710 = 1.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 10 are shuffled. You pick one. What is the probability of a multiple of 3?
items.e: The multiples of 3 are 3, 6 and 9: 3 of the 10 cards, so 310. 13 comes from the word “3”, not from counting cards.

items.q: What is the probability of landing on a prime number?
items.e: The prime numbers are 2, 3, 5 and 7: 4 of the 8 sections, so 48 (= 12). 58 wrongly counts 1, which is not prime. 38 forgets 2.

items.q: A bag has 2 red, 3 blue and 5 green marbles. What is the probability of red or blue?
items.e: Red or blue: 2 + 3 = 5 of the 10 marbles, so 510. 55 compares red and blue with green; it would mean certain.

items.q: Red is in two small parts, each one eighth of the spinner. What is the probability of red?
items.e: 18 + 18 = 28 = 14. 25 counts 2 of the 5 sections, but the sections are not the same size.

items.q: The letters of TORONTO are written on 7 cards. You pick one card without looking. What is the probability of O?
items.e: TORONTO has 7 letters and 3 of them are O: 37. 14 counts the 4 different letters, but O is on 3 cards. 34 compares the 3 O cards with the other 4 cards.

items.q: A 12-sided die has the numbers 1 to 12. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 9, as a percent?
items.e: Greater than 9 means 10, 11 or 12: 312 = 14 = 25%. 3% uses the count as the percent.

items.q: On which spinner is the probability of blue 14?
items.e: On spinner C blue has 2 of the 8 equal sections: 28 = 14. A has 4 sections, but blue is half of it.

items.q: Which bag gives a probability of 0.5 for taking a red marble?
items.e: 0.5 means half of the marbles are red. With 4 red and 4 blue, 4 of 8 are red. 5 red, 10 blue gives 515, not 510.

items.q: A bag has 10 marbles. The probability of red is 25. How many red marbles are there?
items.e: 25 = 410, so 4 of the 10 marbles are red. 2 uses the numerator without changing to tenths. 6 is the number that are not red.

items.q: A bag has 3 green marbles and some blue marbles. The probability of green is 14. How many blue marbles are there?
items.e: 14 = 312, so there are 12 marbles in total. 12 − 3 = 9 blue. 12 is the total, not the number of blue marbles.

sets.title: Two independent events: tables and tree diagrams

items.q: You toss a coin and spin a spinner with 3 equal sections: red, blue and yellow. How many different outcomes are there?
items.e: Each coin face goes with each of the 3 colours: 2 × 3 = 6 outcomes. 5 comes from adding 2 + 3, which is a common mistake.

items.q: The tree diagram shows tossing a coin, then spinning a spinner with 3 equal sections. What is the probability of heads and red?
items.e: Heads and red is 1 of the 6 equally likely outcomes: 16. 15 adds the outcomes (2 + 3) instead of multiplying. 56 adds 12 + 13.

items.q: Use the tree diagram. What is the probability of tails and NOT red?
items.e: Tails and not red: T, blue and T, yellow. That is 2 of 6 outcomes: 26. 46 counts every outcome that is not red, with heads too. 25 adds 2 + 3 outcomes instead of multiplying.

items.q: Use the tree diagram. What is the probability of red, with either heads or tails?
items.e: Red shows up in 2 outcomes: H, red and T, red. So the probability is 26 (= 13), the same as spinning red on its own. 16 forgets T, red. 25 adds 2 + 3 outcomes instead of multiplying.

items.q: You toss a coin and roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. How many different outcomes are there?
items.e: Each coin face goes with each of the 6 numbers: 2 × 6 = 12. 8 comes from adding 2 + 6.

items.q: The table shows every outcome of tossing a coin and rolling a number cube. What is the probability of heads and a 6?
items.e: H6 is 1 of the 12 outcomes in the table: 112. 18 adds 2 + 6 outcomes. 46 adds 12 + 16.

items.q: Use the table. What is the probability of tails and an even number?
items.e: Tails and even: T2, T4 and T6. That is 3 of 12 outcomes: 312 (= 14). 36 only looks at the number cube.

items.q: Use the table. What is the probability of heads and a number greater than 4?
items.e: Heads and greater than 4: H5 and H6. That is 2 of 12 outcomes: 212. 412 also counts T5 and T6.

items.q: A coin is tossed and a spinner with 2 equal sections (red and blue) is spun. Which list shows all the outcomes? (H = heads, T = tails, R = red, B = blue)
items.e: Pair each coin face with each colour: 2 × 2 = 4 outcomes, HR, HB, TR, TB. H, T, R, B lists single results, not pairs. HT is not possible: there is only one coin.

items.q: You spin spinner A and spinner B. How many different outcomes are there?
items.e: Each colour goes with each of the 4 numbers: 2 × 4 = 8. 6 comes from adding 2 + 4.

items.q: You spin both spinners. What is the probability of blue and 4?
items.e: Blue and 4 is 1 of the 8 outcomes (red 1 … blue 4): 18. 16 adds the outcomes (2 + 4). 34 adds 12 + 14.

items.q: Nathan says, “A coin has 2 outcomes and a number cube has 6, so together there are 2 + 6 = 8 outcomes.” What is wrong?
c: Each coin face pairs with all 6 numbers: 2 × 6 = 12
There are only 6 outcomes; the coin does not count
items.e: Heads can go with 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6, and so can tails. That makes 6 + 6 = 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes. Multiply, don’t add.

items.q: You toss two coins. What is the probability of getting one head and one tail?
items.e: The outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. One head and one tail is HT or TH: 24 (= 12). 13 forgets that HT and TH are different outcomes.

items.q: You toss two coins. What is the probability of getting two heads?
items.e: HH is 1 of the 4 outcomes (HH, HT, TH, TT): 14. 13 uses only 3 outcomes (two heads, one of each, two tails), but they are not equally likely. 34 is NOT two heads.

items.q: Mei tosses a coin and gets heads. Then she rolls a number cube. What is the probability that the number cube shows a 6?
items.e: The coin does not change the number cube: the events are independent. A 6 is still 16. 112 is the chance of heads AND 6 before anything is tossed.

items.q: Which two events are independent?
c: Rain this morning and a wet schoolyard at recess
Tossing a coin and spinning a spinner
Practising free throws and making more baskets
Taking two marbles from a bag without putting the first one back
items.e: Two events are independent when one does not change the chance of the other. A coin can’t change a spinner, so tossing a coin and spinning a spinner are independent. Taking a marble out changes what is left in the bag.

items.q: You toss a coin and spin a spinner with 4 equal sections: 1, 2, 3 and 4. What is the probability of tails and an odd number?
items.e: There are 2 × 4 = 8 outcomes. Tails and odd: T1 and T3. So the probability is 28 (= 14). 26 adds 2 + 4 outcomes. 24 only looks at the spinner.

items.q: Use the table. What is the probability of heads and any number from 1 to 6?
items.e: H1, H2, H3, H4, H5 and H6: 6 of the 12 outcomes, so 612 (= 12). It is the same as the chance of heads, because every number is allowed.

items.q: You toss a coin and roll a number cube 120 times. About how many times would you expect heads and a 6?
items.e: Heads and 6 is 1 of 12 outcomes. 112 of 120 is 120 ÷ 12 = 10, so about 10. About 15 comes from 120 ÷ 8 (adding 2 + 6 outcomes).

items.q: Game A: you win if a coin shows heads AND a spinner with 4 equal colours lands on red. Game B: you win if a number cube shows 1 or 2. Which game gives a better chance of winning?
items.e: Game A: heads and red is 1 of 2 × 4 = 8 outcomes, so 18. Game B: 2 of 6 outcomes, so 26 = 13. 13 > 18, so Game B is better.

sets.title: Experimental and theoretical probability: predictions and decisions

items.q: Liam rolls a number cube 60 times. About how many times would he expect to roll a 6?
items.e: A 6 has a theoretical probability of 16. 16 of 60 is 60 ÷ 6 = 10, so about 10.

items.q: Zoe tosses a coin 100 times. How many heads should she expect?
items.e: Half of 100 is 50. Results change from one experiment to the next, so expect about 50, not exactly 50.

items.q: Aiden spins this spinner 40 times. About how many times should he expect red?
items.e: Red is 34 of the spinner. 40 ÷ 4 = 10, and 3 × 10 = 30, so about 30. About 10 is for blue.

items.q: Benjamin tosses a coin 50 times and gets 23 heads. What is the experimental probability of heads?
items.e: Experimental probability = number of times it happened ÷ number of trials = 2350. 12 is the theoretical probability. 2327 compares heads with tails.

items.q: Priya’s class recorded 20 spins. What is the experimental probability of red, as a decimal?
items.e: Red came up 12 times in 20 spins: 1220 = 610 = 0.6. 1.5 comes from 12 ÷ 8 (red ÷ blue), and it is greater than 1.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of yellow, as a percent?
items.e: Yellow came up 10 times in 40 spins: 1040 = 14 = 25%. 10% uses the count as the percent.

items.q: Before each ringette game, a coin is tossed to decide which team starts. Tails has come up 5 games in a row. What is the probability of heads at the next game?
items.e: The coin has no memory. Every toss is a new trial, so heads is still 12. Thinking heads is “due” is called the gambler’s fallacy.

items.q: Kai has rolled a number cube 12 times without getting a 6. What is the probability of a 6 on the next roll?
items.e: The number cube does not remember earlier rolls. A 6 is still 16. It is not certain (1), even after a long wait.

items.q: Ava tosses a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads. Noah tosses a coin 1000 times and gets 508 heads. Whose experimental probability of heads is closer to 12?
items.e: Ava: 710 = 0.7. Noah: 5081000 = 0.508. 0.508 is much closer to 0.5, so Noah’s is closer.

items.q: Why are Noah’s results (1000 tosses) closer to 12 than Ava’s (10 tosses)?
c: More trials usually get closer to the theory
Noah tossed the coin more carefully
Big experiments are always exactly right
items.e: With only a few trials, luck changes the results a lot. More trials usually get closer to the theoretical probability, but not exactly.

items.q: How do these results compare with the theory?
c: The number cube must be unfair
Close: each number should come up about 10 times
4 will come up more next time
items.e: Theory: 16 of 60 = 10 for each number. The results are all between 8 and 12, which is close to the theory. Small differences are normal.

items.q: Leah rolls a number cube 600 times and gets a 6 on 104 rolls. How does this compare with the theory?
items.e: 16 of 600 = 600 ÷ 6 = 100. 104 is close to 100. Experiments are rarely exactly the same as the theory.

items.q: A computer simulates tossing a coin 10 000 times. About how many heads would you expect?
items.e: Half of 10 000 is 5000. A simulation with many trials gets close to the theory, so expect about 5000, not exactly 5000.

items.q: Zoe and Mateo toss a coin and spin a spinner with 3 equal sections (red, blue, yellow) 60 times. They get heads and red 13 times. How does this compare with the theory?
items.e: Heads and red is 1 of 2 × 3 = 6 outcomes. 16 of 60 = 10, and 13 is close to 10. About 12 comes from 60 ÷ 5 (adding 2 + 3 outcomes).

items.q: At hockey practice, Maya’s experimental probability of scoring is 0.32 after 25 shots. How many goals did she score?
items.e: 0.32 × 25 = 8. Check: 825 = 32100 = 0.32. 32 would need 100 shots.

items.q: Ethan counts 40 cars passing the school. 14 of them are white. Estimate the probability that the next car is white.
items.e: 14 ÷ 40 = 35100 = 0.35. 0.65 is the estimate for a car that is NOT white.

items.q: A bag has 20 marbles. Sofia takes one, records its colour and puts it back. She does this 100 times and gets red 26 times. About how many red marbles are in the bag?
items.e: Red came up 26100 = 0.26 of the time, about a quarter. 14 of 20 is 5, so there are about 5 red marbles. 26 is more than the whole bag.

items.q: Three groups spin the same spinner 20 times each. Red comes up 9, 13 and 8 times. Use all the results to estimate the probability of red.
items.e: Add the results: 9 + 13 + 8 = 30 reds in 3 × 20 = 60 spins. 3060 (= 12). Using all 60 spins gives a better estimate than one group. 3020 is greater than 1.

items.q: A spinner has 4 equal sections: red, blue, yellow and green. At the fall fair, red comes up 98 times in 200 spins. What do the results suggest?
c: The spinner is probably not fair
Red will stop coming up soon
200 spins are too few to tell
items.e: Theory: 14 of 200 = 50 reds. 98 is almost double that, after many spins, so the spinner is probably not fair.

items.q: At the school fun fair, Box A has 10 tickets and 3 of them win. Box B has 25 tickets and 7 of them win. Which box gives a better chance of winning?
c: Box B, it has more winning tickets
items.e: Box A: 310 = 30%. Box B: 725 = 28100 = 28%. Box A is better, even though Box B has more winning tickets.
